{{Short description|American mathematician (born 1946)}}
'''Charles Michael''' "'''Chuck'''" '''Newman''' (born 1 March 1946) is a mathematician and a physicist at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] of [[New York University]]. He works in the fields of [[mathematical physics]], [[statistical mechanics]], and [[probability theory]].

He has contributed to numerous fields where probability mixes with physics, including [[metastability]], [[spin glasses]], the mathematics of [[food webs]] and the [[Ising model]], and [[percolation theory]] including its connections to [[Schramm–Loewner evolution]]s and the [[Brownian web]].<ref name="google scholar">{{cite web | title = Chuck Newman's publications on Google Scholar | url = https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?as_q=&num=10&btnG=Search+Scholar&as_epq=&as_oq=&as_eq=&as_occt=any&as_sauthors=CM+Newman&as_publication=&as_ylo=&as_yhi=&as_allsubj=some&as_subj=eng&as_subj=phy&hl=en&lr=&safe=off}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Selected publications (downloadable) of Chuck Newman | url=https://www.math.nyu.edu/faculty/newman/papers.html}}</ref> His work on real zeros of Fourier transforms<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Newman|first1=C.M.|year=1976|title=Fourier Transforms with only Real Zeros|journal=Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.|volume=61|issue=2|pages=245–251|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-1976-0434982-5|zbl=0342.42007|doi-access=free}}</ref> is intimately associated with the Riemann hypothesis, via the [[De Bruijn-Newman constant]].

He is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] since 2004, and of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] since 2006. According to his citation<ref>{{cite web| title=Citation at the National Academy of Sciences| url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/Dir/1888405156?pg=vprof&mbr=1004433&returl=http://www.nasonline.org/site/Dir/1888405156?pg=srch&view=basic&retmk=search_again_link| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604030358/http://www.nasonline.org/site/Dir/1888405156?pg=vprof&mbr=1004433&returl=http:%2F%2Fwww.nasonline.org%2Fsite%2FDir%2F1888405156%3Fpg=srch&view=basic&retmk=search_again_link| url-status=dead| archive-date=June 4, 2011}}</ref> for membership of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], he is "an agile and creative probabilist" who "has made deep, unusually insightful contributions over a wide range of science. He is most widely known for his work in disordered systems, including [[percolation theory|percolation models]], random networks and [[spin glasses]]. His contributions combine conceptual penetration with technical virtuosity".

In 2012, he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-02-24.</ref>

Newman graduated from [[MIT]] in 1966 with degrees in both mathematics and physics. He completed his [[PhD]] at [[Princeton University]] in 1971 with advisor [[Arthur Wightman]].<ref name="mg">{{MathGenealogy |id=11638}}</ref> After two years as an assistant professor at [[NYU]], he accepted a position at [[Indiana University]]. In 1979, he moved to the [[University of Arizona]] in [[Tucson]], and then in 1989 to the [[Courant Institute]]. He was chair of the Mathematics Department from 1998&ndash;2001, and Director of the Institute from 2002&ndash;2006.<ref name=cv>{{cite web | title=Chuck Newman's curriculum vitae | url=https://www.math.nyu.edu/faculty/newman/cv.html}}</ref> His students at NYU have included [[Seema Nanda]].<ref name="mg"/> He is married with two daughters.<ref name=cv/>
